name.text: Probability calculations for an exponential distribution function (copy) (copy)

questiontext.text:
Leaves are falling from a marula tree. The random variable \(X\) measuring the distance of the leaves from the tree is exponentially distributed with average distance {@mean@} meters. Compute

a. The probability of a leaf falling further than {@prob_min_a_disp@} meters from the tree. Give your answer in exact form (recall, the expression \(e^{ax}\) is entered as %e^(a*x) in STACK).

[[input:ans1]] [[validation:ans1]] [[feedback:prt1]]

b. The probability of a leaf falling between {@prob_min_b_disp@} and {@prob_max_b_disp@} meters from the tree. Give your answer in exact form (recall, the expression \(e^{ax}\) is entered as %e^(a*x) in STACK).

[[input:ans2]] [[validation:ans2]] [[feedback:prt2]]

prtcorrect.text: Correct answer, well done.

prtpartiallycorrect.text: Your answer is partially correct.

prtincorrect.text: Incorrect answer.

truefeedback.text:
Worked Solution

Since \(X\) is exponentially distributed with mean {@mean@}, its probability density function is given by

\[f(x) = \frac{1}{{@mean@}} e^{-\frac{1}{{@mean@}}x} = {@mean_recip_disp@}e^{-{@mean_recip_disp@}x}, \]

where \(x\geq 0\).

Therefore, the probability of a leaf falling more than {@prob_min_a_disp@} meters from the tree is

\( \displaystyle P(X \geq {@prob_min_a_disp@}) = \int_{{@prob_min_a_disp@}}^{\infty} f(x) \cdot dx\)

\( \displaystyle \quad \quad = \int_{{@prob_min_a_disp@}}^{\infty} {@mean_recip_disp@}e^{-{@mean_recip_disp@}x} \cdot dx\)

\( \displaystyle \quad \quad = \left[ \frac{{@mean_recip_disp@}e^{-{@mean_recip_disp@}x}}{-{@mean_recip_disp@}} \right]_{{@prob_min_a_disp@}}^{\infty} \)

\( \displaystyle \quad \quad = \left[-e^{-{@mean_recip_disp@}x} \right]_{{@prob_min_a_disp@}}^{\infty} \)

\( \displaystyle \quad \quad = 0 - \left( -e^{-{@mean_recip_disp@}\cdot {@prob_min_a_disp@}} \right) \)

\( \displaystyle \quad \quad = {@ta_1@} \)

\[f(x) = \frac{1}{{@mean@}} e^{-\frac{1}{{@mean@}}x} = {@mean_recip_disp@}e^{-{@mean_recip_disp@}x}, \]

where \(x\geq 0\).

Therefore, the probability of a leaf falling between {@prob_min_b_disp@} and {@prob_max_b_disp@} meters from the tree is

\( \displaystyle P({@prob_min_b_disp@} \geq X \geq {@prob_max_b_disp@}) = \int_{{@prob_min_b_disp@}}^{{@prob_max_b_disp@}} f(x) \cdot dx\)

\( \displaystyle \quad \quad \quad = \int_{{@prob_min_b_disp@}}^{{@prob_max_b_disp@}} {@mean_recip_disp@}e^{-{@mean_recip_disp@}x} \cdot dx\)

\( \displaystyle \quad \quad \quad = \left[ \frac{{@mean_recip_disp@}e^{-{@mean_recip_disp@}x}}{-{@mean_recip_disp@}} \right]_{{@prob_min_b_disp@}}^{{@prob_max_b_disp@}} \)

\( \displaystyle \quad \quad \quad = \left[-e^{-{@mean_recip_disp@}x} \right]_{{@prob_min_b_disp@}}^{{@prob_max_b_disp@}} \)

\( \displaystyle \quad \quad \quad = \left( -e^{-{@mean_recip_disp@}\cdot {@prob_max_b_disp@}} \right) - \left( -e^{-{@mean_recip_disp@}\cdot {@prob_min_b_disp@}} \right) \)

\( \displaystyle \quad \quad \quad = e^{-{@mean_recip*prob_min_b@}} - e^{-{@mean_recip*prob_max_b@}} \)
